questions.question: Distinguish the powers of Masakhane Ltd's shareholders from the duties of its directors, and explain why good governance wants the chairperson and the chief executive to be different people, with the chairperson ideally an independent non-executive director.
questions.expected_answer: Shareholders own the company and exercise their power at the annual general meeting: one vote per share, electing and removing directors, appointing the independent auditor and approving the audit fee, receiving and questioning the annual report, and approving the major decisions reserved for owners. They receive dividends only when declared. Directors manage on the shareholders' behalf under a fiduciary duty: good faith, the company's best interests, no private advantage, and declaration of any personal interest. Their duties include running operations, safeguarding assets through internal control, preparing statements that fairly present, declaring only affordable dividends, and accounting to shareholders at the AGM. The top roles are split because the chairperson leads the board — the body that oversees management — while the chief executive leads the company being overseen. One person holding both jobs would oversee themselves, concentrating the power governance exists to divide. An independent non-executive chairperson, with no other financial ties to the company, can lead that oversight with judgement free of self-interest.

questions.question: A scenario reads: Masakhane's board hid a serious loss from shareholders for a year; during that year a director sold her shares before the loss became public; and the directors set their own pay without disclosure. Name every King Code demand, ethical principle and legal offence involved, and give the remedy for each failure.
questions.expected_answer: Hiding the loss breaches TRANSPARENCY — the board must report openly, bad news with good — and ACCOUNTABILITY, since the board is answerable to shareholders for the true position; the remedy is full, prompt disclosure in the annual report and answering for it at the AGM. The director selling shares on unpublished bad news committed INSIDER TRADING — dealing on information the market lacks, illegal under South African financial markets law — breaching integrity and professional behaviour; the consequences are dismissal, criminal prosecution and, for a professional, expulsion by their professional body. Directors setting their own undisclosed pay breaches FAIRNESS and transparency and ignores the required structure: a REMUNERATION COMMITTEE must set directors' pay so directors never set their own, and that pay must be disclosed director by director in the annual report where shareholders can weigh it against performance. The scenario method throughout is: state the problem from the facts, name the principle or duty broken, recommend the remedy that closes it.

questions.question: Describe the three layers by which a company checks itself — internal control, internal audit and the independent audit — including who operates or appoints each layer and where each reports. Then show the parallel in the Sondela Netball Club story.
questions.expected_answer: Layer one, internal control: management's daily machinery — division of duties so the person who orders never pays and the payer never records, authorisation by approved signature, documentation of every transaction, physical safeguards like safes and passwords, and regular reconciliation of records against reality. The directors carry responsibility for these controls. Layer two, internal audit: employees of the company who test the controls all year and report their findings to the audit committee, not merely to the managers tested, so that an embarrassing finding cannot be buried; internal audit recommends, management remains accountable for acting. Layer three, the independent audit: a registered auditor in public practice, appointed by the shareholders at the AGM, reporting to the shareholders with a published opinion on whether the statements fairly present the position — valuable only while the auditor is independent. In the club: the everyday habits — two signatures on the account, gate money counted, recorded and banked by three different people, receipts and slips for everything — are internal control. Karabo, inside the club and checking all year, reporting gaps to the oversight group rather than to the treasurer she tests, is internal audit. The outside accountant with no ties to the committee, appointed by the members to tell the members whether the treasurer's report is true, is the independent audit. Every arrow points to the owners.
